formulations.label: Solution for injection in pre-filled pen (6 mg/mL, 3 mL)
formulations.strengths: 6 mg/mL (18 mg in 3 mL); doses 0.6 mg, 1.2 mg, 1.8 mg
formulations.note: The original clinic brand has no current UK SmPC on emc; this entry uses UK liraglutide 6 mg/mL pen SmPCs for type 2 diabetes. A weight-management liraglutide product (different doses and indication) is not covered here.

src.q: 1 ml of solution contains 6 mg of liraglutide produced by chemical synthesis. One pre-filled pen contains 18 mg liraglutide in 3ml.
One pre-filled pen contains 18 mg liraglutide in 3 ml.

brandPrescribing.t: SPS: liraglutide is a biological medicine and must be prescribed and dispensed by brand name. The SmPC also asks that the product name and batch number be recorded (traceability).

src.q: Biological medicines such as semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide, and tirzepatide must be prescribed and dispensed by brand name.
In order to improve the traceability of biological medicinal products, the name and the batch number of the administered product should be clearly recorded.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes in adults, adolescents and children aged 10 years and above, with diet and exercise: monotherapy when metformin is inappropriate (intolerance or contraindication), or added to other diabetes medicines.

src.q: Liraglutide is indicated for the treatment of adults, adolescents and children aged 10 years and above with insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise

items.t: SPS: prescribe and dispense by brand name (biological medicine). Only prescribe for licensed indications.

src.q: Biological medicines such as semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide, and tirzepatide must be prescribed and dispensed by brand name.
Only prescribe GLP-1 RAs, or incretin mimetics, for their licensed indication and follow NHS guidance.

items.t: Combination with a sulphonylurea is only valid for adults.

src.q: Combination therapy with sulfonylurea is only valid for adult patients.

items.t: Start 0.6 mg once daily; after at least 1 week increase to 1.2 mg. If needed, after at least another week increase to 1.8 mg. Doses above 1.8 mg daily are not recommended.
items.tag: Type 2 diabetes (adults and children 10 years and over)

src.q: the starting dose is 0.6 mg liraglutide daily. After at least one week, the dose should be increased to 1.2 mg.
after at least one week, the dose can be increased to 1.8 mg to further improve glycaemic control. Daily doses higher than 1.8 mg are not recommended.

items.t: Added to a sulphonylurea or insulin: consider reducing the sulphonylurea or insulin dose; reduce insulin stepwise. Blood glucose self-monitoring is needed to adjust these, especially when starting liraglutide and reducing insulin.

src.q: When Liraglutide is added to a sulfonylurea or insulin, a reduction in the dose of sulfonylurea or insulin should be considered to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia

Blood glucose self-monitoring is necessary to adjust the dose of sulfonylurea and insulin, particularly when liraglutide therapy is started and insulin is reduced. A stepwise approach to insulin dose reduction is recommended.

items.t: Elderly, mild to severe renal impairment, mild or moderate hepatic impairment: no dose adjustment.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required based on age
No dose adjustment is required for patients with mild, moderate or severe renal impairment.

items.t: Children and adolescents 10 years and over: same dosing, no adjustment. No data under 10 years. Combination with a sulphonylurea is for adults only.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required for adolescents and children aged 10 years and above. No data are available for children below 10 years of age
Combination therapy with sulfonylurea is only valid for adult patients.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to liraglutide or any excipient.

src.q: Contraindications Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Should not be used in type 1 diabetes or to treat diabetic ketoacidosis; not a substitute for insulin. Diabetic ketoacidosis has been reported in insulin-dependent patients after rapid stopping or reduction of insulin.

src.q: Liraglutide should not be used in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus or for the treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis. Liraglutide is not a substitute for insulin.
Diabetic ketoacidosis has been reported in insulin-dependent patients after rapid discontinuation or dose reduction of insulin

items.t: Heart failure NYHA class IV: no experience; not recommended.

src.q: There is no therapeutic experience in patients with congestive heart failure New York Heart Association (NYHA) class IV, and liraglutide is therefore not recommended for use in these patients.

items.t: Inflammatory bowel disease and diabetic gastroparesis: not recommended (limited experience; gastrointestinal side effects).

src.q: There is limited experience in patients with inflammatory bowel disease and diabetic gastroparesis.
Use of liraglutide is not recommended in these patients

items.t: General anaesthesia or deep sedation: pulmonary aspiration reported with GLP-1 receptor agonists (delayed gastric emptying); consider before procedures. MHRA: anaesthetists should assess aspiration risk; ask patients about GLP-1 use.

src.q: Cases of pulmonary aspiration have been reported in patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists undergoing general anaesthesia or deep sedation.
anaesthetists should consider the potential risk of aspiration within their risk assessment of patients being treated with GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists

items.t: Acute pancreatitis (including necrotising and fatal cases): caution with a history of pancreatitis (not studied). Stop if suspected; do not restart if confirmed. Raised pancreatic enzymes alone do not predict pancreatitis.

src.q: Liraglutide has not been studied in patients with a history of pancreatitis, and should be used with caution in these patients.
If pancreatitis is suspected, liraglutide should be discontinued. If the diagnosis of pancreatitis is confirmed, liraglutide should not be restarted.
elevations in pancreatic enzymes alone are not predictive of acute pancreatitis

items.t: Pre-existing thyroid disease: use with caution (thyroid events such as goitre reported).

src.q: Thyroid adverse events, such as goitre, have been reported in clinical trials and in particular in patients with pre-existing thyroid disease.
Liraglutide should therefore be used with caution in these patients.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia with a sulphonylurea or insulin: lowered by reducing their dose.

src.q: The risk of hypoglycaemia can be lowered by a reduction in the dose of sulfonylurea or insulin.

items.t: Dehydration, renal impairment and acute renal failure reported: warn patients about fluid loss with gastrointestinal side effects.

src.q: Signs and symptoms of dehydration, including renal impairment and acute renal failure, have been reported in patients treated with liraglutide.
take precautions to avoid fluid depletion

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: a clinically relevant interaction cannot be excluded; monitor INR more often when starting liraglutide.

src.q: A clinically relevant interaction with active substances with poor solubility or with narrow therapeutic index such as warfarin cannot be excluded.
Upon initiation of liraglutide treatment in patients on warfarin or other coumarin derivatives, more frequent monitoring of INR (International Normalised Ratio) is recommended.

items.t: Sulphonylureas or insulin: hypoglycaemia; a dose reduction should be considered. MHRA: diabetic ketoacidosis reported when insulin was rapidly reduced or stopped; reduce insulin stepwise with glucose self-monitoring.

src.q: Patients receiving liraglutide in combination with a sulfonylurea or insulin may have an increased risk of hypoglycaemia
if the insulin dose is to be reduced, a stepwise approach is recommended

items.t: Oral medicines: slightly delayed gastric emptying may affect absorption, but studies showed no clinically relevant delay; no dose adjustment (paracetamol, atorvastatin, digoxin, lisinopril, griseofulvin, oral contraceptives). Severe diarrhoea may affect absorption.

src.q: Interaction studies did not show any clinically relevant delay of absorption and therefore no dose adjustment is required.
Diarrhoea may affect the absorption of concomitant oral medicinal products.

items.t: SPS: use with caution with time-critical or narrow therapeutic window medicines (e.g. levodopa); extra monitoring may be needed.

src.q: Use GLP-1 RAs with caution in people who are taking medicines which are time critical, such as levodopa for Parkinson's disease.
These people may require additional monitoring.

items.t: Mild, moderate or severe renal impairment: no dose adjustment.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required for patients with mild, moderate or severe renal impairment.

items.t: End-stage renal disease: no experience; not recommended. (The SmPC gives no numeric threshold for this.)

src.q: There is no therapeutic experience in patients with end-stage renal disease, and liraglutide is therefore not recommended for use in these patients

items.t: Dehydration from gastrointestinal effects can cause renal impairment or acute renal failure.

src.q: Signs and symptoms of dehydration, including renal impairment and acute renal failure, have been reported in patients treated with liraglutide.

items.t: Mild or moderate: no dose adjustment. Severe hepatic impairment: not recommended.

src.q: No dose adjustment is recommended for patients with mild or moderate hepatic impairment.
Liraglutide is not recommended for use in patients with severe hepatic impairment

items.t: SmPC: should not be used in pregnancy; use insulin instead. Stop if pregnancy is planned or occurs.

src.q: Liraglutide should not be used during pregnancy, and the use of insulin is recommended instead.
If a patient wishes to become pregnant, or pregnancy occurs, treatment with liraglutide should be discontinued.

items.t: BUMPS: GLP-1 receptor agonists should not be used in pregnancy. If used by accident in early pregnancy, available data (about 47,000 pregnancies) are reassuring; no extra monitoring for birth defects is needed.

src.q: GLP-1 receptor agonists should not be used in pregnancy.
If you accidentally used a GLP-1 receptor agonist in early pregnancy, you can be reassured that the available information suggests that it does not harm the baby.
No extra monitoring for major birth defects is required following use in early pregnancy of a GLP-1 receptor agonist.

items.t: SmPC: not known if excreted in human milk; should not be used during breastfeeding (lack of experience).

src.q: Because of lack of experience, liraglutide should not be used during breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: MHRA advise GLP-1 receptor agonists should not be taken while breastfeeding (lack of safety data); contact SPS for patient-specific advice. Insulin or metformin are preferred choices.

src.q: The MHRA advise GLP-1 RAs should not be taken by people who are breastfeeding due to a lack of safety data .
Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.

items.t: SPS: MHRA advise contraception throughout GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment as a precaution. Liraglutide is not expected to reduce oral contraceptive effect.

src.q: They advise contraceptive use throughout GLP-1 RA treatment as a cautionary measure.
The contraceptive effect is therefore anticipated to be unaffected when co-administered with liraglutide.

items.t: Fertility: animal studies showed no harmful effect apart from a slight decrease in live implants.

src.q: Apart from a slight decrease in the number of live implants, animal studies did not indicate harmful effects with respect to fertility.

items.t: Very common: nausea, diarrhoea. Common: vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, headache, nasopharyngitis. Gastrointestinal effects are worse at the start and usually settle within days or weeks.

src.q: nausea and diarrhoea were very common, whereas vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, and dyspepsia were common
Headache and nasopharyngitis were also common.
These reactions usually diminish within a few days or weeks on continued treatment.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: common; very common with a sulphonylurea (severe hypoglycaemia mainly with a sulphonylurea).

src.q: hypoglycaemia was common, and very common when liraglutide is used in combination with a sulfonylurea
Severe hypoglycaemia has primarily been observed when combined with a sulfonylurea.

items.t: Injection site reactions (about 2%), usually mild.

src.q: Injection site reactions have been reported in approximately 2% of patients receiving liraglutide

items.t: Acute pancreatitis, including necrotising and fatal cases: persistent, severe abdominal pain. Stop liraglutide if suspected; do not restart if confirmed. Patients should seek urgent medical attention.

src.q: This includes post-marketing reports of necrotising pancreatitis and reports with a fatal outcome.
if pancreatitis is suspected, discontinue treatment with the GLP-1 or GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist immediately; do not restart therapy if the diagnosis of pancreatitis is confirmed

items.t: Dehydration with renal impairment or acute renal failure (after vomiting/diarrhoea).

src.q: Signs and symptoms of dehydration, including renal impairment and acute renal failure, have been reported in patients treated with liraglutide.

items.t: Anaphylactic reactions and angioedema (few cases); cholelithiasis and cholecystitis; intestinal obstruction.

src.q: Few cases of anaphylactic reactions with additional symptoms such as hypotension, palpitations, dyspnoea and oedema have been reported with marketed use of liraglutide.
Few cases of cholelithiasis (0.4%) and cholecystitis (0.1%) have been reported
Delayed gastric emptying Intestinal obstruction

items.t: Blood glucose self-monitoring is not needed for liraglutide itself, but is needed to adjust sulphonylurea or insulin doses, especially at the start.

src.q: Self-monitoring of blood glucose is not needed in order to adjust the dose of liraglutide.
Blood glucose self-monitoring is necessary to adjust the dose of sulfonylurea and insulin

src.q: more frequent monitoring of INR (International Normalised Ratio) is recommended

src.q: If pancreatitis is suspected, liraglutide should be discontinued.

items.t: Subcutaneous injection once daily at any time, independent of meals, into the abdomen, thigh or upper arm; preferably about the same time each day. Never intravenous or intramuscular.

src.q: Liraglutide must not be administered intravenously or intramuscularly.
Liraglutide is administered once daily at any time, independent of meals, and can be injected subcutaneously in the abdomen, in the thigh or in the upper arm.
it is preferable that liraglutide is injected around the same time of the day

items.t: Rotate injection sites to reduce the risk of amyloid deposits at the site.

src.q: Injection sites should always be rotated in order to reduce the risk of injection site amyloid deposits

items.t: Seek urgent medical help for severe, persistent abdominal pain that may go through to the back, with or without nausea and vomiting (possible pancreatitis).

src.q: seek urgent medical attention if you experience severe, persistent abdominal pain, that may radiate to your back and may be accompanied by nausea and vomiting

items.t: Drink plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration, especially if you have vomiting or diarrhoea.

src.q: throughout treatment stay well hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids (such as water) to avoid dehydration

items.t: Tell your healthcare team and anaesthetist before any surgery or sedation that you use this medicine; do not stop it without discussing with your doctor.

src.q: make sure you inform your healthcare team including the anaesthetist about this prior to your surgical procedure
take your prescribed medicine(s) as usual and do not stop your treatment without first discussing this with your doctor

items.t: If you also use insulin: learn the signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, excessive thirst, passing urine often, difficulty breathing, confusion, unusual tiredness or sleepiness) and get urgent help if they occur.

src.q: Inform patients of the signs and symptoms of diabetic ketoacidosis (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, excessive thirst, increased frequency of urination, difficulty breathing, confusion, unusual fatigue, or sleepiness)

items.t: With a sulphonylurea or insulin, take precautions to avoid low blood sugar while driving.

src.q: Patients should be advised to take precautions to avoid hypoglycaemia while driving and using machines
